extracted.intended_audience: policymakers, education administrators, legal scholars, and stakeholders interested in Title IX rulemaking and administrative process
extracted.subtask_description: Evaluating or producing federal Title IX regulations and related agency policymaking, with attention to procedural form (rulemaking vs guidance), actors who shape policy, legal vulnerability, and effects on regulated institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Responsible actors in rule development
rubrics_metrics.description: Presidents and their appointees, rather than career civil servants, have played the leading role in developing Title IX rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing rulemaking, identify which actors (White House, political appointees, career officials) drove substantive choices; evaluate implications for accountability, responsiveness to administration priorities, and durability across administrations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Judicial influence and litigation risk
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal courts have also played a key role, first expanding and—more recently—blocking the expansion of federal mandates.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess how courts have interpreted, expanded, or enjoined rules; consider likelihood of litigation, regional injunctions, and how judicial decisions affect enforceability and nationwide applicability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of APA formal rulemaking versus informal guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: The US Department of Education’s decision to use the Administrative Procedure Act’s rulemaking procedures rather than rely on unilateral 'Dear Colleague' letters has not only increased the transparency of the policymaking process but also improved the quality of the department’s rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor formal notice-and-comment rulemaking under the APA when possible to enhance transparency, public participation, and perceived legitimacy; evaluate whether the agency followed APA procedures and whether that process improved rule clarity or quality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Bureaucratic enforcement power and oversight
rubrics_metrics.description: The permanent bureaucracy’s greatest power lies not in writing formal regulations but in using investigations that are subject to little public oversight.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine enforcement tools (investigations, compliance reviews) and the degree of public oversight and procedural safeguards; evaluate risks of administrative overreach and the availability of review or appeal mechanisms for investigated parties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive scope and mandates of the rule
rubrics_metrics.description: The new rules are nearly 15,000 words, establishing legally binding mandates on sexual harassment, accommodations for pregnant and lactating students, and treatment of transgender students.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the rule’s length, scope, and the specific substantive obligations it imposes (e.g., harassment definitions, accommodation duties, gender identity treatment); consider whether the rule clearly defines duties and limits of covered institutions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory stability and reversibility across administrations
rubrics_metrics.description: The Biden administration’s rules reversed many provisions of the 2020 regulations issued by the Trump administration, which in turn had overturned policies announced by the Obama administration—indicating the key role the White House and presidential appointees play in the regulatory process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the likelihood that regulatory positions will be reversed with changes in administration; consider mechanisms to increase continuity, such as durable statutory interpretations or bipartisan consensus, and the costs of switching standards for regulated entities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clarity and compliance burden on regulated institutions
rubrics_metrics.description: Soon after the rules were announced, federal courts enjoined their enforcement in half the country—indicating the role the judiciary has long played in developing Title IX rules. Meanwhile, schools throughout the country, from kindergarten to graduate programs, are left uncertain about what they must do to comply with federal law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether rules reduce or increase uncertainty for schools and other entities; analyze administrative burdens, resource implications, and whether the rule provides clear guidance for compliance in diverse educational settings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency of the policymaking process
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of APA rulemaking increased the transparency of the policymaking process.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess the extent to which the rulemaking process was open (notice, comment, responsive rule text, publication of supporting analyses) and whether stakeholders had meaningful opportunity to participate and influence outcomes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multi-factor analysis of administrative policymaking
rubrics_metrics.description: To move beyond overheated rhetoric to 'deconstruct the administrative state,' we must take a closer look at the diverse factors that influence policymaking in particular agencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Conduct a holistic analysis that considers political leadership, agency culture, statutory text, judicial decisions, stakeholder input, enforcement practices, and inter-branch dynamics when evaluating the quality, legitimacy, and likely effects of agency rules.
